title: Boss: monitoring you can trust
summary: Rebuild a health check so its exit code means something, then fix a report that reads only one page and a token that never authenticates.

steps.title: Ticket MON-77
body: *"Last week notify was down for 40 minutes and nobody was paged. The morning report says there are 5 urgent tickets
(the board shows 12). And the capacity dashboard has shown no data since we rotated the API token."*
Monitoring only looks at the exit code; people only read the first line. Make both honest.

steps.title: A health check with a meaningful exit code
prompt: Run `pwsh -File ~/scripts/Test-ServiceHealth.ps1; "exit $LASTEXITCODE"`. Then rewrite it so that, for each service in
the config file (`-ConfigPath`, default `services.json` next to the script):
- it prints exactly **`<name> ok`**, **`<name> degraded`** (the service answered but not with 200), or **`<name> down`**
(no answer, or no answer within **3 seconds**);
- every service is checked, even after one fails;
- it exits **0 only if every service is `ok`**, and **1** otherwise.

checks.name: notify is down: reported, and exit 1
checks.cmd: echo ok > /opt/dojo/state/billing-health; out=$(timeout 25 pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Test-ServiceHealth.ps1 2>/dev/null); rc=$?; echo "$out"; test $rc = 1 && test "$(echo "$out" | tr -d '\r' | sort | tr '\n' ' ')" = 'billing ok notify down orders ok search ok '
checks.fail: With the default config: `orders ok`, `billing ok`, `search ok`, `notify down` (one line each, any order) and exit code 1.

checks.name: billing degraded: reported, and exit 1
checks.cmd: c=$(mktemp); printf '[{"name":"orders","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8091/health"},{"name":"billing","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8092/health"}]' > $c; echo degraded > /opt/dojo/state/billing-health; out=$(timeout 25 pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Test-ServiceHealth.ps1 -ConfigPath $c 2>/dev/null); rc=$?; echo ok > /opt/dojo/state/billing-health; echo "$out"; test $rc = 1 && echo "$out" | grep -qx 'billing degraded' && echo "$out" | grep -qx 'orders ok'
checks.fail: When billing answers 503, print `billing degraded`, still check the rest, and exit 1.

checks.name: all healthy: exit 0
checks.cmd: c=$(mktemp); printf '[{"name":"orders","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8091/health"},{"name":"search","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8093/health"}]' > $c; out=$(timeout 25 pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Test-ServiceHealth.ps1 -ConfigPath $c 2>&1); rc=$?; echo "$out"; test $rc = 0
checks.fail: When every service is ok, the exit code must be 0.

checks.name: a hanging service is down within the timeout
checks.cmd: c=$(mktemp); printf '[{"name":"reports","url":"http://127.0.0.1:8088/slow"}]' > $c; s=$(date +%s); out=$(timeout 20 pwsh -NoProfile -NonInteractive -File ~/scripts/Test-ServiceHealth.ps1 -ConfigPath $c 2>/dev/null); rc=$?; t=$(( $(date +%s) - s )); echo "$out (exit $rc after ${t}s)"; test $rc = 1 && test $t -lt 12 && echo "$out" | grep -qx 'reports down'
checks.fail: A service that does not answer must count as `down` after about 3 seconds (`-TimeoutSec 3`), not hang the check.

hints: Per service: `Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $s.url -TimeoutSec 3 -SkipHttpErrorCheck -StatusCodeVariable code`. With `-SkipHttpErrorCheck` a 503 does not throw; `$code` says what came back.
A connection refused or a timeout still throws: wrap the call in `try { } catch { $state = 'down' }`.
Count the failures in the loop, then `if ($bad -gt 0) { exit 1 }; exit 0`.
solution: # Test-ServiceHealth.ps1: run every minute by the monitoring agent, which pages on-call when the exit code is not 0.
explain: The old script exited 0 whenever its *last* statement succeeded, threw on the first problem (so the services after
it were never checked), and had no timeout, so a hung service hung the monitor too. Monitoring agents (Nagios-style
checks, Task Scheduler, CI health gates) all speak the same language: exit code 0 for healthy, anything else pages.

steps.title: 5 urgent tickets (there are 12)
prompt: `pwsh -File ~/scripts/urgent-report.ps1` prints `urgent: 5`. The board shows 12. Look at what one call returns
(`page`, `next`) and fix the script so it counts the urgent tickets across **all** pages.
hints: One call returns `items`, `page` and `next`: only the first 20 tickets.
Follow `next` until it is `$null`: `$uri = '...'; $tickets = while ($uri) { $p = Invoke-RestMethod -Uri $uri -Headers $headers -TimeoutSec 10; $p.items; $uri = $p.next }`.
Replace the `$tickets = ...` line with that loop.
steps.explain: When a count is "suspiciously round" or equals the page size, pagination is the first suspect. Many APIs also let you ask the server to filter (`?priority=urgent`), which is faster than downloading everything and filtering on your side.

steps.title: The format of value 'Bearer ...' is invalid
prompt: Since the token was rotated, `pwsh -File ~/scripts/ticket-count.ps1` fails before it even reaches the server. Read
the error carefully (where does the quoted value end?), fix the script, and make it print `tickets: 47`.

checks.name: the token stays out of the script
checks.fail: Do not paste the token into the script: keep reading it from `~/.config/ops/api-token`.

hints: The error shows the header value with a line break before the closing quote: the token file ends with a newline, and `Get-Content -Raw` keeps it.
HTTP header values may not contain line breaks, so .NET refuses to send the request at all.
explain: The old token was written without a final newline; the new one, by a different tool, with one. `Get-Content` without
`-Raw` (one string per line) or `.Trim()` avoids it. The lasting fix is a secret store instead of a file: module 7
uses `Get-Secret`, which returns exactly the value that was stored.
